title: Debugging a Model That Will Not Learn
interviewAnswer: Verify data and labels, then try to overfit a tiny batch. Inspect loss, outputs, gradients, learning rate, preprocessing and train/eval modes before changing architecture. Debug from simplest assumptions outward.
why: Debugging questions reveal whether you can work independently when a model fails rather than randomly changing hyperparameters.
intuition: Debug from the simplest possible failure outward: verify data and labels, then prove the model can overfit a tiny batch, then inspect gradients/loss/learning rate, then scale complexity.
deepDive: Check shapes, dtypes, normalization, label alignment and train/eval modes. Overfit one batch: if the model cannot drive training loss down, there is likely a pipeline, optimization or capacity bug. Inspect baseline loss, output ranges, gradient norms and which parameters receive gradients. Disable augmentation/regularization, simplify the model, compare against a trivial baseline, then reintroduce complexity one piece at a time.
workedExample: If binary classification loss stays near 0.693, inspect whether logits vary, labels are correct, gradients are nonzero and the optimizer actually owns the model parameters before increasing network depth.
code:
# Tiny-batch sanity test
x,y=next(iter(loader))
for _ in range(500):
    opt.zero_grad(); loss=criterion(model(x),y)
    loss.backward(); opt.step()
print(loss.item())
commonMistakes: Changing model architecture before verifying labels/data.
Debugging training and validation problems simultaneously.
Leaving dropout/augmentation on while trying to prove the pipeline can overfit a tiny batch.
followUps: What if gradients are all zero?
Training loss decreases but validation worsens—what next?
production: Capture reproducible configs, seeds, logs, sample inputs, checkpoints and environment versions so failures can be reproduced instead of debugged from memory.
